body.title: Sacred Boulders and River Coracles: The Kishkindha Landscape Across Millennia
body.orientation: How woven bamboo coracles and ancient granite outcrops preserved the sacred river boundary of the Vijayanagara Empire.

hero.alt: Circular woven coracles floating on the Tungabhadra River near ancient Hampi boulders

paragraphs.text: The Tungabhadra River cuts through one of the oldest exposed granite landscapes on earth, dividing the ancient monkey kingdom of Kishkindha from the imperial capital of Vijayanagara.
For centuries, local boatmen have navigated its treacherous rapids using circular woven coracles (harigolu), made from split bamboo waterproofed with leather or tar.
Sixteenth-century Portuguese chronicler Domingo Paes documented these very basket-boats transporting warriors, horses, and temple supplies across the river.
Coracle navigation on the Tungabhadra represents an unbroken living watercraft technology, linking modern travellers directly to medieval river life.

followUpQuestions: How does the coracle's circular shape prevent it from tipping in river whirlpools?
What mythological sites in Kishkindha are reachable only by river crossing?

claims.text: The Tungabhadra river passes through Precambrian granite boulder hills associated with the Kishkindha of epic tradition.

evidence.excerpt: The Tungabhadra River flows past Hampi through steep granite gorges traditionally identified with Kishkindha.

claims.text: Coracles are circular woven wickercraft vessels constructed for navigating turbulent river waters.

evidence.excerpt: Coracles made of woven bamboo reeds and waterproofed hide have been used as ferries across the Tungabhadra for centuries.

claims.text: Domingo Paes and other early European visitors recorded the widespread use of coracles in Vijayanagara.

evidence.excerpt: Portuguese traveler Domingo Paes noted that people crossed the river in round basket-boats that could carry ten men and horses.

claims.text: Coracle ferrying continues today as an active community tradition at Anegundi and Hampi.

evidence.excerpt: Modern travelers and pilgrims continue to use coracles to cross the river between Hampi and Anegundi.
